title: Liver transplantation as a treatment for cancer: comprehensive review
question: Which cancers can be treated with liver transplantation, and how well do carefully selected patients do?

bottom_line.question: Which cancers can be treated with liver transplantation, and how well do carefully selected patients do?
bottom_line.answer: Liver transplantation is now an option for selected patients with several liver cancers. In the only randomised trial, for unresectable colorectal liver metastases, 5-year survival was 56.6% with transplant plus chemotherapy versus 12.6% with chemotherapy alone.

provenance.quote: After a median follow-up of 59.3 months, the 5-year intention-to-treat survival in the LT cohort was 56.6% in the transplant group compared with 12.6% in the chemotherapy group.

sections.title: Transplant as a Cancer Treatment
sections.markdown:
## Cancer as a reason to replace a liver

Liver transplantation is usually thought of as a fix for a failing liver. For a growing group of patients it is a cancer treatment: surgeons remove the whole liver, tumours included, and put in a healthy one. This field is called **transplant oncology**, the treatment of cancer through transplant medicine and surgery. The review collects the current evidence for each cancer where transplant is used, the technical problems involved, and how centres cope with a shortage of donor livers. It is written for clinicians in specialist centres.

Four judgements shape any decision. Resectability asks whether the tumour can be cut out while leaving enough liver behind. It is less objective than it sounds, because techniques that make the remaining liver grow before surgery are applied under different rules at different centres. Operability asks whether the patient is fit enough to survive surgery. Curability asks whether they will stay free of disease, often judged as no recurrence at 5 years. Transplantability asks whether they meet the rules for the waiting list. Those rules weigh the chance of dropping off the list, the risk of death after transplant, and how many organs are available. Donor livers are scarce, so giving one to a patient whose cancer may return raises an ethical question about allocation.

The review's main yardstick is **transplant benefit**, the survival a transplant adds over the best non-transplant option:

transplant benefit = survival after transplant - survival with the best alternative treatment

The International Liver Transplantation Society (ILTS) consensus says this should be one of the main factors in deciding who qualifies.

Living donor liver transplantation (LDLT), in which a healthy person gives part of their liver, has become important in this field. It bypasses the waiting list and lets surgeons time the operation around chemotherapy. The cost is the risk to a healthy donor.

sections.title: Colorectal Metastases and Bile Duct Cancers
sections.markdown:
## Colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver

About half of people with colorectal cancer develop metastases, most often in the liver. Surgically removing these colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) is the only cure. Even so, 75 to 80% of patients cannot have surgery and receive palliative chemotherapy instead, and only about 10% of them are alive at 5 years.

The SECA-I trial (2013) was the first controlled test of transplant for CRLM that could not be removed surgically. Estimated overall survival (OS) was 95% at 1 year, 68% at 3 years and 60% at 5 years. Only 35% of patients were cancer-free at 1 year. Most recurrences, though, were slow-growing lung metastases that surgeons could remove, so patients lived long anyway.

SECA-I identified four features linked to worse survival: a largest tumour over 5.5 cm, less than 2 years since the bowel cancer surgery, a CEA blood marker above 80 micrograms per litre, and cancer that kept growing during chemotherapy. Each feature scores one point in the **Oslo score**:

Oslo score = number of these four risk factors present (0 to 4)

Ten-year data published in 2022 showed that patients scoring 0 or 1 had actual survival of 75% at 5 years and 50% at 10 years. The follow-up SECA-II trial used stricter entry rules and reached estimated OS of 100%, 83% and 83% at 1, 3 and 5 years. Disease-free survival (DFS) was still only 35% at 3 years, yet survival after recurrence was 73% at 4 years. For this cancer, DFS is a poor measure of whether transplant works, because recurrence is often treatable.

The Oslo score alone is not enough to pick candidates. Other warning signs are a primary tumour on the right side of the colon, a BRAF mutation, and undifferentiated or signet ring cell tumours. A PET/CT scan is used to rule out spread outside the liver. A metabolic tumour volume under 70 cubic centimetres on that scan strongly predicts good survival, and the authors recommend measuring it routinely.

The strongest evidence comes from TransMet, a randomized trial of transplant plus chemotherapy against chemotherapy alone in patients with heavy disease (a median of 20 metastases). At 5 years:

- counting every randomized patient (intention to treat): 56.6% alive with transplant vs 12.6% with chemotherapy
- counting only those who received their assigned treatment (per protocol): 73.3% vs 9.3%

This makes CRLM the only transplant oncology indication supported by level 1 evidence, the highest grade.

As more centres adopt the approach, donor livers become the bottleneck. Living donation is common in Asia and rarer in the West. The RAPID procedure, introduced in 2015, stretches the supply. Surgeons remove the left side of the patient's liver, implant a small piece of donor liver (segments 2 and 3), and divert portal blood flow to the graft so it grows quickly. Once the graft is big enough, usually 2 to 3 weeks later, they remove the rest of the diseased liver. A study across seven European centres found RAPID safe, with the second operation at a median of 2 weeks. The graft can come from a split deceased donor liver or from a living donor. With a living donor, the donor gives a smaller piece (lower risk) while the recipient still gains a lot. This works because CRLM patients usually have otherwise healthy livers without portal hypertension, so they manage with smaller grafts than typical transplant patients.

## Hilar cholangiocarcinoma

Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (hCCA) is a bile duct cancer at the point where the ducts leave the liver. Thomas Starzl first transplanted it in 1963. Of the eight patients his group treated up to the mid-1980s, five survived past 2 months, and four of those five died of recurrence. The approach was nearly abandoned. The authors blame poor patient selection and the lack of strict chemotherapy before transplant.

The Mayo Clinic protocol (2000) changed this by giving chemotherapy with radiation before transplant. Of 11 transplanted patients, only one recurred, and median survival was 44 months. A 2004 follow-up of 28 patients reported 82% survival at 5 years and a 14.2% recurrence rate.

### Who qualifies

The Mayo rules were later adopted by the US allocation body UNOS. Under them:

- the tumour must be unresectable and diagnosed by brush cytology from the duct
- it must be under 3 cm and/or cause a malignant-looking narrowing with a CA19-9 marker above 100 U/ml
- the patient must not have had prior surgical exploration or a needle biopsy through the skin

Brush samples often miss cancer cells, and adding a genetic test (FISH) improves accuracy. Lymph nodes are biopsied by endoscopic ultrasound before treatment starts, because any spread rules out transplant.

### Treatment before transplant

Chemoradiation before transplant (neoadjuvant therapy) shrinks the tumour and lowers recurrence. It also tests tumour biology: cancers that progress despite treatment are too aggressive to benefit. The original scheme gave external radiation with 5-FU, then radiation inside the bile duct, then capecitabine until transplant. Centres now differ in how they give radiation, and some use gemcitabine with cisplatin. Trials in advanced biliary cancer showed that adding the immunotherapy drugs durvalumab (2022) or pembrolizumab (2023) improves survival. Immunotherapy cannot be given after transplant because it would trigger rejection, so the authors think it reasonable to add it beforehand.

### Surgery

Before listing, surgeons sample the lymph nodes at the entrance to the liver, often by keyhole or robotic surgery. About 28% of patients without primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC, a chronic bile duct disease) turn out to have nodal or distant spread at this stage. Centres differ on when to do this staging operation, and no data show that timing affects outcome.

sections.title: Neuroendocrine, Liver Cell and Vascular Tumours
sections.markdown:
## Neuroendocrine tumour liver metastases

Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) are rare, about 0.5% of all cancers, and usually slow-growing. Most patients eventually develop liver metastases, often in both lobes. Removing as much tumour as possible prolongs life and eases hormone symptoms. When the spread is too diffuse to remove, transplant has been proposed as a cure.

The evidence comes mostly from registries and single centres. European registry data show 5-year survival of 47 to 70%. Patients transplanted after 2000 did better (59% at 5 years) than earlier patients (46%). The improvement came from better selection, as centres learned which features predict poor results: disease outside the liver, removing the primary tumour at the same time as the transplant, and vascular or nodal involvement.

In 2016 the Milan group reported 5-year and 10-year survival of 97% and 89%. Their criteria are now the standard in most programmes:

- a low-grade tumour (Ki67 below 10%)
- a primary tumour that drains into the portal vein and was fully removed beforehand
- no more than half the liver involved
- stable or responding disease for at least 6 months
- age 55 or younger (later raised to 60)

Transplant added an estimated 6.82 months of survival over 5 years and 38.43 months over 10 years.

A 2021 comparison of patients within the Milan criteria found 10-year survival of 93% after transplant versus 75% after resection, and 10-year DFS of 52% versus 18%. A propensity-matched study, which pairs similar patients to reduce bias, found 10-year survival of 88.8% with transplant versus 22.4% with resection. European (ENETS) guidelines describe transplant as an option in highly selected, preferably young patients whose hormone symptoms resist medical therapy. It is still unclear how lutetium-177 radionuclide therapy fits in, either as an alternative to transplant or before it. The authors call for a prospective trial.

## Hepatocellular carcinoma

About 90% of hepatocellular carcinomas (HCC) arise in a damaged or cirrhotic liver. The causes include hepatitis B or C, alcohol, and metabolic fatty liver disease (MASLD). Unlike the other cancers in this review, HCC is driven by the diseased liver itself. It also tends to appear in several places at once: 50 to 60% of livers removed at transplant contain multiple tumours, and at least 30% of these were missed on scans. Transplant removes both the tumours and the organ that produced them. That is why it gives the best long-term results for HCC that is confined to the liver and has not invaded major vessels.

### Early HCC

The Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) system has guided HCC treatment for three decades. For very early tumours (a single tumour of 2 cm or less), ablation, which destroys the tumour with heat, works as well as surgery. For early tumours (up to three nodules of 3 cm or less), resection or ablation is offered to patients without significant portal hypertension or who cannot have a transplant. Transplant gives the best results, especially for patients within the size-based Milan or UCSF criteria.

One strategy is to resect first and transplant only if the cancer comes back ("salvage" transplant). It performs poorly, because only 33% of patients who recur actually get a curative transplant. For a single tumour up to 3 cm, resection matches transplant and beats ablation. For multiple tumours or tumours of 3 to 5 cm, transplant is probably best. If transplant is not possible, chemoembolization (TACE) combined with microwave ablation works better than either one alone.

### Intermediate-stage HCC

Most patients arrive with large or multiple tumours, and the MASLD epidemic has added more late-presenting, aggressive cases. Until 2022, the BCLC system offered these intermediate-stage (BCLC B) patients only non-curative therapy.

It turned out that well-selected patients beyond the Milan and UCSF limits survive about as well after transplant. Large series using expanded criteria (tumours up to 7.5 cm, up to three in number) report acceptable long-term results. Asian centres led this push because deceased donor livers are scarcer there, and patients would lose their chance while waiting. The focus moved away from tumour size and count, toward whether the cancer has spread outside the liver or into major vessels.

What matters most is tumour biology, meaning how aggressively the cancer behaves. The markers used include:

- blood levels of AFP and PIVKA-II, and how they change
- how brightly tumours light up on PET scans
- how the disease behaves over a waiting period (the "test of time")
- inflammatory blood ratios and tumour grade

Successful **downstaging** is itself a sign of favourable biology. It means shrinking the tumour with TACE, radioembolization (TARE) or radiotherapy until it meets the criteria.

This work led the 2022 BCLC update to recommend transplant for the first time in selected stage B patients, using extended criteria that include tumour size and AFP. The update also introduced "treatment stage migration", which lets doctors use another stage's treatment when the first-line option does not suit the patient.

Vitale and colleagues showed that transplant gives the largest benefit to patients with advanced cirrhosis and BCLC stage B or C HCC without spread outside the liver, because these patients lack good alternatives. Expanding the criteria lowers long-term survival by 10 to 15%, but results remain better than ablation or drug therapy. In the authors' own study, transplant added 42 months of survival over 5 years compared with TACE or TARE in patients at low risk of recurrence, and 25 months even in high-risk patients.

sections.title: Anti-Rejection Drugs, Donor Livers and Follow-up
sections.markdown:
## Do anti-rejection drugs help cancer return?

Transplant patients need drugs to prevent rejection, and those drugs may weaken the body's defences against cancer. Most of the evidence comes from HCC.

Calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs), namely cyclosporin and tacrolimus, are the backbone of most regimens. They appear to help tumours grow by raising growth signals such as VEGF. High blood levels (cyclosporin above 300 ng/ml, tacrolimus above 10 ng/ml) independently predict HCC recurrence. A CNI given alone carries more risk than a CNI combined with other drugs. With cyclosporin, the risk tracks the cumulative dose, especially in months 4 to 12 after transplant. With tacrolimus, the effect shows only in the first month, and the reason for the difference is unclear.

mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus and everolimus) block a growth pathway and the formation of new tumour blood vessels. Compared with CNI regimens, they are linked to better survival and less recurrence. Adding sirolimus to a CNI improved recurrence-free survival for up to 5 years. In the only randomized trial, the benefit lasted up to 5 years, was largest in low-risk patients, and was greatest with sirolimus alone. Steroids, azathioprine and antibody induction drugs show no link to recurrence. Most of this evidence is retrospective, and the one trial had few patients on sirolimus alone. The authors therefore say firm recommendations must wait for prospective trials.

## Organ shortage and machine perfusion

At some centres, up to 20% of patients die on the waiting list. Donors are older and more often diabetic or obese, and cancer indications add to demand. Centres increasingly use two kinds of higher-risk liver: livers from donors after circulatory death (DCD) and "marginal" livers from brain-dead donors (DBD).

DCD livers carry higher risks of injury when blood flow returns, of grafts that never work, and of bile duct scarring. ILTS describes an ideal donor as aged 60 or younger, with a BMI of 30 or under, less than 30% fat in the liver, and less than 8 hours of cold storage. None of these limits is absolute. For DCD donors, the functional warm ischaemia time should not exceed 30 minutes. This interval runs from the moment oxygen saturation falls below 80% or blood pressure below 60 mmHg until the liver is flushed with cold fluid. Up to 50% of marginal DBD livers are declined.

Machine perfusion pumps fluid through a liver outside the body, and it is changing which livers can be used:

- Normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) keeps the liver at body temperature so its function can be tested before transplant. In the VITTAL trial it allowed 71% of previously discarded livers to be transplanted, with 100% patient and graft survival at 90 days.
- Hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (HOPE) runs cold (4 to 10 degrees C), oxygenated fluid through the liver. This slows metabolism and reduces damage when blood flow returns. In a European randomized trial of DCD livers, the dual-vessel version (D-HOPE) cut bile duct strictures by 64% and early graft dysfunction by 39%.
- Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) restores blood flow in the donor's abdomen before the organs are retrieved. Its results are comparable to standard DBD livers.

Early data suggest HOPE may lower HCC recurrence. Perfusion also lets centres schedule transplants during the day. That helps in transplant oncology, where tissue samples are checked by frozen section pathology during the operation.

## Follow-up

Follow-up aims to catch recurrence early, especially when only a few spots appear that can be treated directly. One experienced unit treated HCC recurrence after living donor transplant with combined therapies and reported 57% survival at 1 year and 24% at 3 years. Its longest survivor lived 7.5 years after recurrence. A sample HCC protocol uses:

- CT every 6 months for 2 years, then yearly
- ultrasound every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months
- AFP or PIVKA-II blood tests every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months

Where resources are tight, risk scores such as SIMAP500 can focus the intensive schedule on high-risk patients.

sections.title: Where the Field Is Heading
sections.markdown:
## Where this leaves the field

Cancer is now an established reason for liver transplantation. Across all these cancers, selection is moving from measuring tumours toward reading their biology. The authors expect radiomics (data extracted from medical scans), tumour genomics, and circulating tumour DNA and RNA to push this further. Colorectal liver metastases are the only indication with randomized trial evidence. For the others, the authors see international prospective registries as the practical way to overcome small patient numbers and build stronger evidence.

sources.zraf034-s2.1/p5: A recent randomized clinical trial, TransMet, has compared liver transplantation + chemotherapy to chemotherapy alone in patients with unresectable CRLM. The study population had a high tumour load with a median of 20 metastases in both groups, and the delay from diagnosis to randomization was 15.9 months in the transplant arm. All transplanted patients but one had a low Oslo-score (<2). After a median follow-up of 59.3 months, the 5-year intention-to-treat survival in the LT cohort was 56.6% in the transplant group compared with 12.6% in the chemotherapy group. In per-protocol analysis, the corresponding 5-year survival rates were 73.3% and 9.3%. The outcomes of the TRANSMET trial confirm the principal findings from all the previous clinical trials on LT for CRLM and have the potential to change clinical practice since CRLM is the only transplant oncology indication that is supported by level 1 evidence.
sources.zraf034-s2.1/p2: The first controlled ‘proof of concept’ SEcondary CAncer (SECA-I) trial to explore LT in non-resectable CRLM was published in 2013 and found an estimated overall survival (OS) of 95%, 68% and 60% at 1, 3 and 5 years respectively. However, disease-free survival (DFS) was only 35% at 1 year. Still, most recurrences were slow-growing lung metastases that could be offered curative intent resection, thereby yielding a favourable overall survival despite recurrence post-transplant. Risk factors for inferior survival were maximal tumour diameter >5.5 cm, time from primary cancer surgery <2 years, CEA levels >80 μg/l and disease progression after chemotherapy at the time of LT. The four factors constitute the ‘Oslo-Score’ by assigning 1 point to each for risk stratification. The 10-year outcome data of the SECA-I trial was published in 2022 and showed that a low Oslo score of 0–1 is associated with a 5-year and 10-year actual OS of 75 and 50% respectively.
sources.zraf034-s2.1/p3: In a follow-up study (SECA-II), the Oslo score factors were considered in the design of the inclusion criteria but were not applied directly. The study cohort, following more stringent inclusion criteria, resulted in Oslo scores of 02, and the estimated 1-, 3- and 5-year OS was 100%, 83% and 83% respectively. Median DFS was 53%, 44% and 35% at 1, 2 and 3 years respectively and about 70% of the recurrences observed were lung metastases where a majority could be offered resection. The OS after recurrence was 100%, 73% and 73% at 1, 2 and 4 years respectively, indicating the DFS has limitations as a parameter of treatment efficacy in liver transplantation for CRLM.
sources.zraf034-s2.4/p4: Long-term outcomes were published in 2021, comparing the patients who underwent liver resection with curative intent and liver transplantation within the Milan criteria. Resection was offered to patients considered radically resectable and transplantation to unresectable. The 5-year and 10-year OS were 95 and 93% for transplant cohort, 90% and 75% for resection cohort (P = 0.007). The 5-year and 10-year DFS rates were 75 and 52% for LT and 33 and 18% for LR (P < 0.001). The median disease-free interval between liver surgery and recurrence was longer in the transplant cohort compared to resection cohort (78 versus 24 months, P < 0.001). Transplant patients showed a tendency for multisite recurrence, while resected patients for intrahepatic recurrence. This study might suggest that any patient with disease presentation meeting the Milan criteria may achieve a significant survival advantage with LT. A propensity score-matched study of resection versus transplantation for the patients within the Milan criteria demonstrated superior survival and disease control in the LT group with 88.8% 10-year OS and 13.1% disease progression compared with 22.4 and 89% respectively, in the resection group.
sources.zraf034-s2.6/p3: Meanwhile, Lai et al. established a prognostic scoring system by analysing the outcomes of 149 recipients undergoing LT for HEHE between 1984 and 2014 in the ELTR-ELITA registry. The 5-year post-LT OS and DFS rates were 79.5% and 79.4% respectively. The disease recurred in 37 (24.8%) patients after a median time of 18 months. Macrovascular invasion detected at pathology (HR 4.9; 95% c.i. 2.4–9.9), pre-LT waiting time ≤120 days (HR 2.5; 95% c.i. 1.2–5.3) and hilar lymph node invasion (HR 2.2; 95% c.i. 1.1–4.5) but not extrahepatic metastases, were found to be significant risk factors for post-LT recurrence. The HEHE-LT score was developed based on these three factors that successfully stratified the patients into three groups by their 5-year DFS rates: low score (0–2), 93.9% (n = 58), intermediate score (3–5), 76.9% (n = 74) and high score (6–10), 38.5% (n = 17). In 2020, the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) held a virtual consensus meeting involving >80 experts to reach a global consensus on HEHE management. This meeting concluded that LT for unresectable HEHE with no extrahepatic disease should be offered to patients ‘after full disclosure of the potential benefits and the risks’ associated with LT (level V evidence, Grade A recommendation).
sources.zraf034-s2.6.1/p3: Calcineurin inhibitors (CNIs), such as cyclosporin and tacrolimus, have long been used in immunosuppressive regimens post-transplantation. CNIs have been shown to create an environment which enables tumour development and growth. For example, they increase the expression of transforming growth factor-β and vascular endothelial growth factor, both of which are known to promote HCC tumourigenesis,. Several studies have shown that high CNI exposure is an independent risk factor for HCC recurrence and reduced recurrence-free survival. In these studies, high concentrations were defined as cyclosporin trough concentration of >300 ng/ml and tacrolimus trough concentration of >10 ng/ml. Further evidence of CNIs alone increasing HCC recurrence risk was shown in a large US retrospective cohort study with CNI monotherapy having a significantly increased risk compared with a combined CNI, antimetabolite and steroid immunosuppression regimen. Furthermore, cumulative dose exposure to cyclosporin has been shown to increase HCC recurrence post-transplant and reduce 5-year recurrence-free survival, particularly when these higher doses are administered in the 4–12 month interval post-transplantation. In contrast, these differences have only been observed in the first month with patients exposed to high-dose tacrolimus, with no significant difference noted after that,. The underlying reason for these differences between cyclosporin and tacrolimus is unclear and needs further assessment in larger prospective clinical trials.
sources.zraf034-s2.6.1/p4: In contrast to CNIs, mTORi, including sirolimus and everolimus, have antiangiogenic and antineoplastic effects by inhibiting the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway and reducing expression of vascular endothelial growth factor, resulting in reduced carcinogenesis. Clinical studies comparing mTORi to tacrolimus-based immunosuppressive protocols showed statistically significant improved overall survival and reduced HCC recurrence in those receiving sirolimus. This was also observed in studies in which cyclosporin or tacrolimus was used as the CNI agent, compared with sirolimus-only immunosuppression therapy,. It appears to be a potential class effect as similar significant differences in HCC recurrence and survival have been observed with everolimus compared with CNIs. Furthermore, the combined sirolimus/CNI regimen had significantly improved recurrence-free survival up to 5 years compared with the CNI-only regimen, suggesting potential antagonism of the known procarcinogenic effects of CNI in HCC recurrence and antitumour advantage. Interestingly, in a large retrospective registry-based cohort study, sirolimus survival benefit was greater in patients transplanted for HCC than patients without HCC, suggesting a specific benefit for the HCC cohort post-transplant. In the only randomized clinical trial, recurrence-free survival and OS were noted up to 5 years post-transplantation, particularly in those with low risk of HCC recurrence, and the greatest recurrence-free survival and OS was noted in those patients on sirolimus monotherapy compared with combined immunosuppression regimens.
sources.zraf034-s1/p3: Transplant benefit is defined as the gain offered by liver transplantation (LT) compared with the best alternative therapy (survival after LT minus survival with the best alternative treatment). The International Liver Transplantation Society (ILTS) Consensus guidelines on Transplant Oncology emphasized that transplant benefit should be one of the key parameters to be considered when defining optimal selection criteria for LT.
